summary:
Aegis Health is an autonomous physiological monitoring dashboard for astronauts on long-duration deep space missions such as Lunar Gateway and Mars transit. Astronauts log six daily vitals: resting heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, core temperature, sleep duration, and mood/psychological readiness. A triage engine classifies each vital as Green (nominal), Yellow (warning) or Red (urgent) and escalates the overall status to Red if any single vital is Red. The dashboard shows a composite health index from 0 to 100, compares readings against pre-flight baselines, and keeps a searchable, exportable history of past assessments. It runs entirely in the browser with no server connection, and all thresholds sit in one configuration file so medical researchers can update them without touching code.

It addresses the challenge by giving crews a way to track their own health and get plain-language feedback when communication with Earth is delayed or lost. This matters because on deep space missions, astronauts can't count on real-time guidance from flight surgeons. Early detection of physiological decline, backed by accessible color-and-icon indicators, supports safer decisions and healthier crews far from home.
details:
Aegis Health: Project Details

What it does and how it works

Aegis Health is a browser-based health dashboard for astronauts on deep space missions. The astronaut completes a short daily assessment covering six indicators: resting heart rate, blood pressure (systolic/diastolic), blood glucose, core body temperature, sleep duration, and mood/psychological readiness (Optimal, Nominal, Fatigued, Stressed, Disoriented). Every field shows its unit, enforces numeric limits, and includes a short microgravity-specific explanation of why the vital matters.

A status engine (healthStatus.ts) compares each value against configurable thresholds and assigns Green, Yellow or Red, with a plain-language reason for each result. Triage follows medical priority: if any single vital is Red, the overall status becomes Red. The dashboard shows:

  • an overall triage banner with a 0–100 composite health index
  • six indicator cards
  • a daily compliance tracker (assessment logged or pending)
  • a recent telemetry feed

The History page keeps a chronological archive that can be searched by Sol, symptoms or notes, filtered by status, inspected in a detail modal, and exported as JSON. The Overview page compares the pre-flight baseline, the latest reading and the operational target for each vital. All data is stored in the browser's LocalStorage, so the app works with no network connection.

Benefits

  • Autonomy: Crews get immediate, understandable feedback when Earth communication is delayed or interrupted.
  • Early warning: Tracking against personal baselines, not just population averages, can reveal gradual decline sooner.
  • Accessibility: Status uses icons and text as well as color, so color-blind users can read it.
  • Maintainability: Medical experts can update all thresholds in one file without touching UI code.
  • Reliability: 35 automated tests verify the triage logic.

Intended impact

The goal is to support crew safety and decision-making on missions where real-time flight surgeon support isn't guaranteed, and to make self-monitoring a simple daily routine. Phase 1 is a prototype and a foundation for a fuller on-board health system, not a medical device.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages and frameworks: TypeScript 5.6, React 18.3
  • Build tool: Vite 5.4
  • Styling: Tailwind CSS 3.4 with a custom space dark-mode palette
  • Icons: Lucide React
  • Charts: Recharts 2.13, configured for Phase 2 trend visualization
  • Storage: Browser LocalStorage with seeded demonstration data
  • Deployment and workflow: Git/GitHub, Vercel configuration, Node.js scripts for automated testing
  • Hardware: Runs on any standard laptop or device with a modern browser. No special hardware is required.

Creativity

  • The interface is styled as a mission-control cockpit, with a live UTC clock, Mission Elapsed Time and "Sol"-based records.
  • The Nominal/Warning/Critical prefill buttons let anyone see the full triage behavior in seconds.
  • Thresholds are separated from the interface, so the app can be tuned by clinicians as well as developers.
  • The offline-first design is built around the real constraint of communication delay.

Factors our team considered

  • Communication delay: The app must work independently of Earth.
  • Medical safety: Triage is deliberately conservative, escalating to the worst status. Thresholds are labeled provisional and the app carries a clear disclaimer that it doesn't replace flight surgeons or certified equipment.
  • Accessibility and usability: Astronauts are tired and busy, so the interface needs clear units, validation and short explanations.
  • Team collaboration: We split the work into phases. Phase 1 covers the core system. Phase 2 (planned) adds an interactive body map, trend charts, a guidance engine and mission routines. Phase 3 covers visual polish. The medical research lead curates the thresholds.
  • Scalability: The modular structure and typed interfaces let new indicators and features be added without rewriting the core.
